warnings: ICMR-NIN 2020 chromium 50 µg/day was seen only in secondary summaries (secondary, unverified); EAR, TUL and pregnancy, lactation and 60+ values Not found.
No upper limit is set by US NASEM/NIH or EFSA; FitPlate shows a soft supplement caution at 250 µg/day (est.; secondary, unverified sources).
IFCT chromium values look too high for staples (rice 5, atta 6, milk 4 µg/100 g vs about 1 µg/100 g or less in independent surveys; secondary) and are whole numbers; show chromium as approximate.
IFCT 0 means not analysed, not zero (eggs, chicken, ghee, oils); do not count as zero.
Do not use IFCT paneer (110), khoa (119) or black amaranth seed (1,227 µg/100 g) for chromium; they look like analysis or contamination errors.
Stainless-steel cookware can add chromium to acidic dishes; food values for tomato or tamarind gravies may be inflated.
Chromium may add to diabetes medicines (low blood sugar) and may reduce levothyroxine absorption; follow your doctor's advice.
Chromium supplements are not recommended by ADA for blood sugar control without a deficiency; do not stop diabetes medicines.
Chromium(III) in food is not the same as hexavalent chromium(VI), an industrial pollutant.
Never show a low-chromium warning; deficiency is documented only in long-term intravenous feeding.
